extracted.intended_audience: scholars and graduate students in philosophy of mathematics and foundations of mathematics; historians of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and characterizing the methodological and epistemological criteria Hilbert used in axiomatizing geometry (e.g., choice and grouping of axioms, independence, modelling, completeness, ideal elements) as discussed in a philosophy-of-mathematics chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin axiomatization from a domain of 'facts' [Tatsachen]
rubrics_metrics.description: Axiomatization should start from a certain domain of 'facts'—what over time has come to be accepted (from proofs, observations, empirical investigations), not necessarily only empirical facts or established truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert describes picking certain 'basic facts' from intuition, experience, or accumulated proofs as the starting point; different sets of basic facts may be chosen depending on purpose. These 'facts' motivate which axioms are adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group axioms by natural conceptual divisions corresponding to levels of empirical/intuitive justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms should be organized into groups (e.g., incidence, order, congruence; then parallels and continuity) that reflect conceptual unity and different degrees of empirical/constructible character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert groups I–III (incidence, order, congruence) as 'very simple' and easily demonstrable by finite experiments, while IV (Parallel) and V (Archimedean/continuity) demand more experimental confirmation; independence results underline such distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of method: derive propositions solely from a specified restricted set of axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that a proposition P (or development T) can be deduced using only a circumscribed stock of principles (the 'restricted methods'), thereby showing the epistemological source of that result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This echoes Euclid's practice of withholding stronger assumptions (e.g., the Parallel Postulate) and is used to display that certain results follow from only limited axioms; Hilbert continues such investigations (e.g., congruence, proportion, area) to show what can be achieved without stronger assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence analysis: show that propositions cannot be deduced from given axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate the converse task of purity of method: show that P (or T) cannot be deduced solely from a specified set of axioms (or can be deduced only with a strengthening), i.e., prove independence results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert's novelty is focusing on unprovability/independence via modelling/translating the theory into other theories. Examples include independence of the Parallel Axiom or Archimedean Axiom and showing that new observations are needed to establish some intuitive facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modelling/interpretation: primitive concepts must be free for reinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: In independence and consistency investigations, primitive terms should not be tied to their usual intuitive meanings; axioms are a 'schema of concepts' that may be filled in many ways by interpretations (models).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert stresses separating basic terms from ordinary associations so that different models can be built; this freedom enables independence proofs and shows that no interpretation of an axiom system is privileged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of axioms and drawing precise logical consequences despite inexact applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Even though physical/empirical applications of axioms are only approximate, axioms must be taken precisely and their precise logical consequences derived to obtain a coherent logical overview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert notes that in physics and practical geometry axioms hold only approximately; nevertheless one must formalize axioms exactly to carry out logical deductions. Example: replace macroscopic bodies by smaller grains or threads so axioms are satisfied under interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness/adequacy with respect to analytic geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory synthetic axiomatization should be 'complete' in the sense of proving all geometrical results that analytic (coordinate) geometry can prove — an adequacy requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert imposed an adequacy condition: synthetic axiomatization ought to be able to recover the results obtainable by analytic geometry (coordinatization by reals); he uses completeness as an adequacy check while still aiming to keep synthetic methods independent where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence via consistency and modelling (consistency-as-existence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical theory 'exists' if it is free from contradiction; demonstrating existence is done by providing a model (e.g., a real-number model for completed Euclidean geometry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert treats 'existence' of mathematical objects as relative to a consistent system: if one can model the axioms in e.g. the real numbers, then the geometric system 'exists'. Disputes about 'real' existence of certain points are considered idle in this framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of introducing ideal elements for methodological purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is methodologically acceptable to introduce ideal objects (e.g., irrational points) that extend a core system to gain analytic power, provided the extension satisfies the axioms and can be modelled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert introduces 'ideal (irrational) points' to complete systems and develop analytic geometry; their 'actual' existence is irrelevant—their use is a matter of method to obtain fuller development (and justified by consistency/model existence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emancipation from intuition: separate logical investigation from empirical origins
rubrics_metrics.description: Axiomatization should allow the study of logical relationships among propositions independently from the empirical or intuitive truth of the axioms; mathematics is a 'projection into the conceptual sphere.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert argues that even though geometry has empirical roots, mature axiomatic method separates logical interconnections from questions of actual truth, enabling the investigation of theories as pure conceptual frameworks (Gedankengebilde).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple and manifold interpretations are desirable
rubrics_metrics.description: A good axiomatic approach recognizes many possible interpretations of the same schema of concepts; the more connections to the world (interpretations), the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert emphasises that theories can be applied in many ways; different applications (interpretations) can show the usefulness of a theory even if none is privileged. This supports modelling and the freedom to choose interpretations for proofs or applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness expectation: internal logical apparatus must be reliable
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit in the method is the assumption that the logical apparatus is sound: if the axioms hold under an interpretation, then the theorems follow under that interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert assumes that once axioms are satisfied in a model, the derived propositions are also satisfied; this underwrites the use of models to demonstrate consistency/existence and to transfer theorems to interpreted domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge approximate/inexact nature of physical interpretation and adjust applications
rubrics_metrics.description: When interpreting axioms physically, accept that applications hold only approximately and that one may need to refine the interpretation (e.g., using smaller grains, thinner wires) to better satisfy axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert gives explicit examples of how to interpret points/lines by physical bodies and how to adjust when propositions aren't precisely satisfied; this grounds axioms in observation but retains the idealized formal system as primary for deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse which axioms/auxiliary means are necessary for given proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematically investigate which axioms or auxiliary assumptions are required to prove particular geometrical facts (i.e., determine necessity and sufficiency relations among axioms and theorems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert phrases this as 'cast[ing] light on which axioms, assumptions or auxiliary means are necessary in the proof of certain elementary geometrical truths' and uses it to show both sufficiency (purity of method) and necessity (independence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid introducing extraneous assumptions foreign to the subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use unnecessarily strong or 'foreign' assumptions (e.g., full differentiability or treating lengths implicitly as magnitudes) if weaker, more intrinsic assumptions suffice to develop the theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert criticises uses like Lie's reliance on differentiable functions as 'foreign to the subject matter' and praises deriving magnitude theory intrinsically rather than imposing extra assumptions as Euclid was sometimes implicitly charged with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and compare different ideal extensions (incompatible but existent if consistent)
rubrics_metrics.description: A core axiomatic system may have many distinct ideal extensions (completions) that are incompatible with each other; each such extension 'exists' insofar as it is consistent and can be modelled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert notes that elementary geometry admits various incompatible ideal extensions, some yielding non-Euclidean geometries; comparing these is part of foundational work and all are legitimate if they are consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: View axiomatization as mapping a domain of knowledge onto a conceptual framework
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal axiomatization is a procedure that maps objects and relations from some domain of knowledge onto an abstract framework of concepts; the theory is a schema to be 'filled with material.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert describes axiomatization as 'projection into the conceptual sphere' and as providing a schema whose concepts correspond to objects in applications; this justifies freeing axioms from fixed intuitive meanings and encourages systematic comparison of different fillings.
